---
title: "Turning a question into a comparison"
---

How much higher is F1 in *hid* /ɪ/ than in *heed* /i/ for the speakers in the Hillenbrand study? A numerical subtraction is interpretable only after its unit, response, linguistic contrast, comparison, and target have been specified consistently.

We name those five ingredients, construct the paired speaker differences, and then contrast the resulting estimand with a different question asked of the same records.

We continue with the [Hillenbrand vowel table introduced on the preceding page](linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key). One row is one /hVd/ token nested within a speaker; [aggregation can remove](linguistic-data.qmd#what-aggregation-removes) the speaker pairing that the present contrast needs. Hillenbrand et al. (1995) used the measurements to compare vowel acoustics and identification; the smaller analysis here isolates one paired acoustic contrast without attempting to reproduce their discriminant analyses.

```{r}
#| label: load-paired-vowels
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv("data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv")
pair_long <- subset(vowels, vowel %in% c("i", "I"),
                    select = c(speaker_id, speaker_type, vowel, f1_hz))

heed <- subset(pair_long, vowel == "i",
               select = c(speaker_id, speaker_type, f1_hz))
hid <- subset(pair_long, vowel == "I",
              select = c(speaker_id, f1_hz))
names(heed)[names(heed) == "f1_hz"] <- "heed_f1_hz"
names(hid)[names(hid) == "f1_hz"] <- "hid_f1_hz"

pairs <- merge(heed, hid, by = "speaker_id", all = FALSE)
pairs$difference_hz <- pairs$hid_f1_hz - pairs$heed_f1_hz

stopifnot(
  nrow(pairs) == length(unique(vowels$speaker_id)),
  !anyDuplicated(pairs$speaker_id),
  all(pairs$difference_hz == pairs$hid_f1_hz - pairs$heed_f1_hz)
)
```

## Response and linguistic contrast

The [**response**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms) is steady-state F1 in hertz. The predictor is vowel category, restricted to the intended vowels /i/ and /ɪ/. Because each of the `r nrow(pairs)` speakers produced both vowels, the comparison is within speaker.

A response specification should name what was measured, its units, and the token at which it was measured:

> The response is steady-state first-formant frequency in hertz for one /hVd/ vowel token.

The release's F1 values were measured at a time judged maximally steady. They are not trajectories over the full vowel.

F1 is the lowest major vocal-tract resonance. It tends to vary inversely with
vowel height, so the /ɪ/–/i/ comparison asks how two nearby front-vowel
categories differ acoustically under the same /hVd/ elicitation frame.

## Observations being compared

The paired difference for speaker $s$ is

$$
d_s
\equiv
F1_{s,\text{/ɪ/}}-F1_{s,\text{/i/}}.
$$

This subtraction holds the speaker fixed. Comparing two unpaired vowel means would produce the same difference of sample means in this complete balanced table, but it would discard the design fact that the two measurements came from the same vocal tract.

For speaker 1, the two source rows become one derived row by matching on
`speaker_id`; `difference_hz` is then `hid_f1_hz - heed_f1_hz`. The sample
summary repeats that operation for all 139 speakers and averages the resulting <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
$d_s$ values:

$$
d_1=F1_{1,\text{/ɪ/}}-F1_{1,\text{/i/}},
\qquad
\bar d=\frac{d_1+\cdots+d_{139}}{139}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: summarize-paired-vowels
mean_difference <- mean(pairs$difference_hz)
median_difference <- median(pairs$difference_hz)
positive_proportion <- mean(pairs$difference_hz > 0)

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    mean_difference,
    mean(pairs$hid_f1_hz) - mean(pairs$heed_f1_hz)
  )),
  positive_proportion >= 0,
  positive_proportion <= 1
)

c(mean_difference_hz = mean_difference,
  median_difference_hz = median_difference,
  proportion_positive = positive_proportion)
```

The observed mean paired difference is `r round(mean_difference, 1)` Hz, and `r scales::percent(positive_proportion, accuracy = 0.1)` of speakers have a positive difference. Both summaries are computed from speaker-level contrasts, but they answer different questions about magnitude and directional consistency.

```{r}
#| label: plot-paired-vowels
#| fig-cap: "Speaker-level F1 differences for /ɪ/ minus /i/. The blue line marks the observed mean paired difference."
ggplot(pairs, aes(difference_hz)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "grey78", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_difference,
             color = "#2C7FB8", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "F1 difference: /ɪ/ minus /i/ (Hz)", y = "Speakers") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## State the estimand

Let $\mu_d$ be the population mean of the within-speaker difference under the elicitation and measurement protocol. The target is

$$
\tau
\equiv
\mu_d
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[
F1_{s,\text{/ɪ/}}-F1_{s,\text{/i/}}
\right].
$$

The sample mean $\bar d$ estimates this target:

$$
\bar d
\equiv
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}d_s.
$$

The displayed difference describes the study's sampled speakers. Generalizing it to new speakers requires an account of how the sampled talkers represent a target population; the original study reports that most were raised in Michigan's Lower Peninsula.

## The same records, a different question

The same rows can support at least three distinct questions: (i) how F1 differs between /i/ and /ɪ/, (ii) how duration differs between those vowels, and (iii) whether speakers with larger F1 contrasts also have larger duration contrasts. The first two have acoustic measurements as responses, while the third concerns an association between two speaker-level contrasts. Thus shared records do not imply a shared estimand.

Three alignment failures recur in linguistic analysis. First, a token-level dataset may be interpreted as if it contained independent speakers. Second, a predictor may confound the intended contrast with different lexical items or talker groups. Third, evaluation on already observed speakers may be described as prediction for new speakers. None of these failures can be repaired merely by changing the estimator.

The mean difference becomes interpretable because the unit, response, within-speaker comparison, and target have been stated. The [Zipf page](zipfs-law.qmd) next applies the same discipline to a corpus-level pattern.

## Test the distinction

1. Use `pairs` to compute the mean F1 for each vowel and verify the displayed identity for $\bar d$.
2. Replace F1 with `duration_ms`, construct the paired differences, and state the resulting response and estimand.
3. Compute the mean F1 difference separately for each `speaker_type`. Why do those descriptive values not by themselves identify age or sex as a cause?
4. A student replaces the 278 token rows with two vowel means before pairing. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
   Which quantity can still be computed, and which information has been lost?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Mean F1 is 411.568 Hz for /i/ and 476.072 Hz for /ɪ/, so the mean of the 139 within-speaker differences is $476.072-411.568=64.504$ Hz. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. With duration as the response, the estimand is the mean within-speaker duration difference, /ɪ/ minus /i/, which is $-55.734$ ms in these data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Mean F1 differences are 74.741 Hz for boys, 41.526 Hz for girls, 86.667 Hz for men, and 47.063 Hz for women; these observational summaries do not isolate age or sex. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The difference between the two grand means can still be computed, but the
   139 speaker-specific differences and their variation have been removed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The measurement-to-estimand chain now has three levels: F1 in hertz is the
token-level response, $d_s$ is the speaker-level paired contrast, and $\mu_d$
is the target mean contrast under the stated protocol. The [Zipf
page](zipfs-law.qmd) next applies the same alignment discipline to corpus
counts, ranks, and a descriptive curve.
